newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. State economy is rebounding -Fed's McDonough.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. State economy is rebounding -Fed's McDonough.

text.p: President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York William McDonough said the New York State economy is staging a comeback that is likely to result in the creation of some 80,000 new jobs next year.
Speaking to a group of business leaders in Rochester, New York, McDonough said compared to the nation as a whole, regional economic growth "has come more grudgingly."

"The 1990-1991 U.S. recession hit New York State harder and lasted longer than was the case in most of the rest of the country," the New York Fed chief said in his prepared remarks, a copy of which was released here.

Large scale restructuring in the financial services sector, continued downsizing in manufacturing and defense-related industries, and the bursting of the bubble of real estate values all contributed to the region's plodding advance, McDonough said.
But the area is bouncing back, he noted.
Trade and services sectors have flourished; new jobs in health-related and social services continue to grow, and job counts in many smaller industries have also advanced, he said.
The construction industry also has shown more signs of life. New home sales are up and prices have risen, he said.

"Job growth in New York State is likely to continue its gradual recovery. Despite the likelihood of some moderation in national economic growth in 1997, economists at the New York Fed believe that the State's job growth rate will accelerate modestly to 1.0 percent from 0.8 percent in 1996," he said.
Stated differently, McDonough said that equates to roughly 80,000 new jobs to be added to New York payrolls next year.
Still, the New York Fed chief said consolidation in the banking sector will continue to slow growth in the region.

In addition, recently enacted welfare reform legislation could increase projected state budget deficits, as local governments strive to provide other assistance to recipients who lose federal benefits, he added.
